nodes.label: Health index
nodes.notes:
The health score consists of six inputs in total.
The score has a base value of 85. To reach a score of 100 (the ideal health condition of the intersection), players need to bring each metric below its penalty threshold and ensure a high index of active mobility: (amount of bikes p/h + amount of pedestrians p/h) / total flow of people.
Thresholds are described within each input.
The index is built up in the following manner:

Active mobility share above 80%: +15
NO₂ above 60 µg/m³: −20
PM2.5 above 25 µg/m³: −30
Noise level above 77.5 dB: −15
Heat level above 39 °C: −15
Speed level of 30–50 km/h (speed-limit-induced accident rate change): −5

— — —

Shapes follow the literature: PM2.5 concave/supralinear; NO₂ linear; noise convex; heat convex; active mobility saturating; accidents via Elvik/Nilsson power curve on telemetry speed. Two inputs added — greenery→health (non-thermal benefit, +5) and avg_speed telemetry driving accidents. Max magnitudes preserved (PM2.5 −30, NO₂ −20, noise −15, heat −15, accidents −5, active mobility +15, greenery +5).

nodes.label: PM2.5
nodes.notes:
The model uses a single linear formula calibrated against a verified Berlin reference measurement:
PM25 = 10.4 + 0.00235 × veh/h
The background term (10.4 µg/m³) is the BLUME inner-city background and implicitly contains today's mixed ICE fleet contribution to city-wide PM2.5. The rate (0.00235 µg/m³ per veh/h) is derived from the traffic-attributable delta at a Berlin inner-city intersection with 1,105 veh/h reference flow (Berlin Environmental Atlas, SenMVKU 2024). It represents a relative scaling factor, not an absolute per-vehicle emission factor.
Fleet scenario corrections are applied as a flat offset on top of the base formula:
PM25 = 10.4 + 0.00235 × veh/h           // current ICE fleet (default)
PM25 = 10.4 + 0.00235 × veh/h - 2.16   // fully electric private fleet city-wide
PM25 = 7.8  + 0.00235 × veh/h           // transit-only (electric buses and trams)
The -2.16 µg/m³ EV correction represents the exhaust-attributable fraction of current PM2.5, derived from EU-average source apportionment (ICARUS: 27% traffic share in urban background; EEA 2023: 40% exhaust / 60% non-exhaust). The transit-only baseline of 7.8 µg/m³ replaces the background term and reflects the theoretical no-private-traffic floor (7.59 µg/m³) plus a small residual for electric transit non-exhaust. Both corrections are stated assumptions based on EU averages rather than Berlin-specific measurements and should be treated as indicative rather than precise.

nodes.label: trams per hour
nodes.notes:
VALUE CORRECTED 2026-09-05 from 10 to 6, to agree with this node's own note below: the M8 timetable gives a 10-minute peak headway, which is 6 trains per hour per direction, and the 720 passengers/h the note derives is 6 x 200 x 60 per cent. 10 contradicted the research recorded on the node and was reachable by nothing - the node had no formula and no edges. It is now the tram's service-frequency lever, the counterpart of bus_frequency_h, and feeds mob_attract_tram. Whether it should become an active slider the player can move is an open question for the author; bus_frequency_h is passive, so this mirrors it.

M8 Tram — Realistic Hourly Passenger Throughput
The M8 operates with Bombardier Flexity Berlin (30 m) vehicles, each with a nominal capacity of approximately 200 passengers (70 seated, ~130 standing at 4 p/m²).
During peak hours (06:00–09:00 and 13:30–19:30, Mon–Fri), the timetable provides a 10-minute headway at U Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz, yielding 6 trains per hour per direction. Applying a 60% occupancy rate — deliberately below the contractual ceiling of 65% defined in BVG's service agreement with the Berlin Senate — gives a realistic throughput of:
6 trains × 200 passengers × 60% = ~720 passengers/hour/direction
The 60% figure is consistent with the Senate's characterisation of M8 peak demand as "deutlich hoch" (significantly high) without constituting structural overload. Note that published BVG occupancy figures are daily averages across the full route; inner-city sections during rush hour regularly exceed this. A further operational caveat: the M8 recorded an on-time rate of only 79.4% in 2024, meaning load distribution across vehicles is less uniform than the timetable implies.

nodes.label: substitutable_fraction
nodes.notes:
Share of through-demand that converts to LOCAL WALKING trips, structurally capped at 6%. Used by effective_trip_demand = traffic_demand_input x (1 - substitutable_fraction).
WHY IT SATURATES (concave; half-life = 20 DDI points): built-environment elasticities for walking are small and DIMINISHING - each added increment of destination access yields less than the last. Ewing & Cervero (2010), 'Travel and the Built Environment: A Meta-Analysis', JAPA 76(3), doi:10.1080/01944361003766766.
WHY DIVERSITY (not quantity) DRIVES IT: substitution is bounded by trip PURPOSE - a 2nd supermarket adds almost nothing, but a 1st school / gym / pharmacy each unlocks a new substitutable trip class. Land-use diversity/entropy is an independent walk driver: Cervero & Kockelman (1997), 'Travel demand and the 3Ds', Transp. Res. D 2(3), doi:10.1016/S1361-9209(97)00009-6.
6% CEILING: ~6.1% of all trips are locally substitutable by walking when destination density improves - Berlin SrV 2018 / MiD 2017, short-trip (<3 km) share.
Formula: min(0.06, 0.06 * (1 - 0.5^(DDI/20))). Reads destination_density_index, which is built from the distinct typologies (new_typologies) + ground-floor activity (space_activity_index).

A shelter alone (about 2 minutes) matched +5 points against the measured ridership gain, so the stop is about four times that: +15 to +20. The access curve in bus_stop_access agrees: the first stop there is worth 19.9. amount_of_cars->noise_level.notes:
Noise Calculation – Methodology
The calculation of the sound level is based on the German standard RLS-90 (Guidelines for Noise Protection along Roads, Federal Ministry of Transport, 1990 edition), the mandatory calculation method in accordance with the 16th Federal Immission Control Ordinance (BImSchV). The basic formula Lm(25) = 37.3 + 10 × log10(M) describes the emission level at a distance of 25 m as a logarithmic function of the hourly vehicle equivalents. For the model, the formula was abstracted to y = b + 10 × log10(x) and calibrated to a target value of 75 dB(A) using real traffic data from Torstraße in Berlin (average daily traffic of 26,520 vehicles, 2019 traffic survey)—in accordance with the official Berlin noise map for 2022. Trucks and buses were weighted as passenger car equivalents using the RLS-90 factor ×10, and the daily traffic volume (DTV) was extrapolated to a representative peak hour using a factor of 1.5. The resulting baseline b = 41.5 applies to façade levels at a height of 4 m on a four-lane main street in Berlin’s inner city area. The temporal distribution of traffic volume throughout the day follows the HBS (Handbook for the Design of Road Traffic Facilities): The relevant peak hour accounts for 10% of the AADT, which amounts to ~2,650 vehicles/h for Torstraße and corresponds to a façade level of ~75.7 dB(A). At night (2–5 a.m.), the volume drops to ~0.5% of the ADT (~130 vehicles/h), which corresponds to a level of ~64.5 dB(A)—still well above the WHO nighttime limit of 45 dB Lnigh

The per-vehicle emission rates are calibrated against a single real-world reference point: annual mean pollutant concentrations measured at a Berlin inner-city intersection with a daily traffic volume of 26,520 vehicles (DTV 2019, Verkehrsmengenk­arte Berlin), equivalent to approximately 1,105 vehicles per hour. At this reference traffic load, NO₂ reaches 28.0 µg/m³ and PM₂.₅ reaches 13.0 µg/m³ (Berlin Environmental Atlas, Modelldaten 2024, SenMVKU). Subtracting the respective background concentrations yields the traffic-attributable delta: 9.0 µg/m³ for NO₂ and 2.6 µg/m³ for PM₂.₅. Dividing by the reference flow produces the emission rates used in the model: 0.00814 µg/m³ per veh/h for NO₂ and 0.00235 µg/m³ per veh/h for PM₂.₅. These rates represent a linear scaling relative to a verified real-world baseline, not absolute per-vehicle emission factors, and are therefore valid for relative comparisons within the simulation rather than for absolute dispersion modelling.

noise_level->public_space_quality.notes:
Noise Level & Public Space Attractiveness — Design Rationale
Penalty thresholds are set at 55 dB (−5), 65 dB (−10), and 75 dB (−15), corresponding to the WHO's established annoyance and health-effect breakpoints for outdoor environments. Below 55 dB, speech intelligibility and perceived restorativeness are unimpaired. Above 55 dB serious annoyance begins; above 65 dB restorative value degrades substantially; above 75 dB the space becomes actively hostile to leisure use with documented cardiovascular stress responses.

noise_level->health_index.notes:
Two distinct health dimensions are modelled. For health impact: cardiovascular risk begins at 53 dB Lden (IHD risk +8% per 10 dB, high certainty, WHO ENG 2018); 65 dB marks loss of acoustic comfort for 20% of the EU population; 70 dB is the EPA lifetime hearing loss threshold; above 80 dB, hearing impairment risk becomes acute

— — —
[2026-07-05] Live scoring converted from steps to a continuous convex (accelerating) curve: penalty = min(15, 15·((L−53)/27)^1.8). Zero at 53 dB, −15 at 80 dB. Convexity reflects the log-linear IHD risk per 10 dB (WHO ENG 2018) and cubic-spline annoyance functions — harm rises slowly through the mid-range and steeply near 75–80 dB.

temperature->health_index.notes:
Heat Levels
A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis (Lancet) quantifies cardiovascular mortality risk increasing by 2.1% per °C, and by 17% during heatwaves. Thresholds are calibrated to Berlin's climate: 30°C is a warm but normal summer day; 35°C is rare; 40°C corresponds to the historical 99th percentile — an extreme event with disproportionate health impact. Penalties (0 / −3 / −8 / −13 / −15) reflect this non-linear escalation.

— — —
[2026-07-05] Live scoring converted from steps to a continuous convex (accelerating) heat curve: penalty = min(15, 15·((T−28)/12)^1.7). Zero at 28 °C, −15 at 40 °C. Matches the J-shaped temperature-mortality curve whose heat arm accelerates toward extremes (Gasparrini et al. 2015, Lancet). The cold arm is intentionally not modelled (out of scope).

temperature->public_space_quality.source: Fan et al. 2023; UTCI (Brode et al. 2012); Nikolopoulou & Lykoudis 2006.
temperature->public_space_quality.notes:
Penalty thresholds are set at 30 °C (−5), 35 °C (−10), and ≥38 °C (−15), reflecting empirically measured activity drops of 5%, 13%, and near-maximum depression respectively. The urban heat island modifier and greenery interaction are included because urban parks face both higher ambient temperatures and amplified activity sensitivity. The secondary wellbeing penalty at sustained 30 °C+ reflects a documented ~27-minute delay in evening activity with established links to circadian disruption.

[2026-07-05] Curve redesign: live PSQ node_formula supersedes the old threshold penalty with a continuous thermal comfort gate: exp(-0.5*pow((temperature-22)/(temperature>=22?18:14),2)). Centered at 22 C with asymmetric warm/cool tolerances from outdoor activity and UTCI comfort evidence.

formula.label: Inert provenance edge; live PSQ node_formula applies empirical thermal comfort gate

pm25->health_index.notes:
Thresholds follow the WHO 2021 Global Air Quality Guidelines Interim Targets, which quantify mortality directly: relative mortality at AQG (5 µg/m³) = 100; at IT4 (10 µg/m³) = 104; IT3 (15 µg/m³) = 108; IT2 (25 µg/m³) = 116; IT1 (>25 µg/m³) = 124. Penalties (0 / −8 / −16 / −24 / −30) scale linearly from this mortality table. Causality between PM2.5 and all-cause, cardiovascular, respiratory and lung cancer mortality is rated high certainty by WHO.

— — —
[2026-07-05] Live scoring converted from the step ladder to a continuous concave (supralinear) curve: penalty = min(30, 30·((PM2.5−5)/20)^0.6). Zero at the 5 µg/m³ WHO-AQG reference, −30 at 25 µg/m³; passes through the old anchors (−20 at 15, −30 at 25) but front-loads harm near the clean floor, matching cohort/GEMM evidence that the concentration-response is steepest at low levels with no threshold (Burnett et al. 2018, PNAS; 'How low can you go?', Science Advances 2022). Caveat: some low-end supralinearity may be measurement-error artifact (Environ. Epidemiol. 2024), so curvature is kept moderate (exponent 0.6). The step figures above are retained for reference.

formula.label: PM2.5 concave/supralinear penalty, 0 at 5, -30 at 25 µg/m³

no2->health_index.notes: [2026-07-05] Continuous linear ramp: penalty = min(20, 0.37·(NO₂−6)). Zero at the ~6 µg/m³ decarbonised background, −20 at ~60 µg/m³. NO₂-mortality is log-linear/near-linear with no clear threshold — this is the one genuine ramp among the toxins (Huangfu & Atkinson 2020, cohort meta-analysis, ~1.02 per 10 µg/m³ all-cause mortality).

active_mobility_index->health_index.notes:
Four thresholds reflect the non-linear dose-response relationship between active mobility and all-cause mortality (Kelly et al., 2014; WHO Europe, 2022). Benefits are front-loaded: the transition from sedentary to any meaningful active mobility yields the largest marginal gain (+8), with diminishing returns at higher shares. The final threshold (>78) captures near-complete modal shift, where evidence shows 30% lower cancer mortality among bike commuters. Maximum cumulative bonus: +20 points.

— — —
[2026-07-05] Live scoring converted from steps to a continuous saturating curve: bonus = 16·(1−exp(−share/35)) ≈ +7 at 20%, +13 at 60%, ~+15 near full modal shift. Front-loaded diminishing-returns shape, consistent with the Kelly et al. 2014 physical-activity dose-response.

blue_infrastructure->temperature.source: Jacobs, Klok, Bruse, Cortesão, Lenzholzer & Kluck 2020, Are urban water bodies really cooling?, Urban Climate 32:100607, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.uclim.2020.100607; Völker et al. 2013, Erdkunde 67(4):355–371, https://www.erdkunde.uni-bonn.de/article/view/2737; Ulpiani et al. 2019 (mist field test), https://iris.univpm.it/handle/11566/265086
blue_infrastructure->temperature.notes: 2026-10-29 (greenery on the 11,500 m² map): Slope −0.3 → −0.1 °C per unit. blue_infrastructure is a plaza module with 0–2 units, so both features give −0.2 °C. The old −6 °C maximum (20 units × −0.3) had no source and was a balance choice to reach 28 °C on a heat day. Evidence: small urban water bodies cool the air around them by about 0.2 °C on average in the afternoon, 0.6 °C at most, and are negligible in design practice (Jacobs et al. 2020, ENVI-met, REALCOOL). The 2.5 K (95 % CI 1.9–3.2) of Völker et al. 2013 is for large lakes and rivers, not plaza features. Misting and spray systems cool 2–10 °C (8.2 °C in Ulpiani et al. 2019) but only downwind, while running, and less in wind or high humidity: a local felt effect, not junction-wide air temperature. Water can also raise humidity and slightly warm the junction at night. Effects of two features are taken as additive, which is generous. Old note: NORMALIZED: max_available_units=20 | max_node_impact=−6°C | slope = max_node_impact / max_available_units = −6 / 20 = −0.300. To change the spawn ceiling, update max_available_units and recalculate slope accordingly. Rationale: 20 water features (fountains, channels, parklet water elements) at full deployment. Evaporative cooling effect, second-strongest cooling source after greenery.

formula.label: −0.1 °C per water feature, −0.2 °C for both (typical small still water, Jacobs et al. 2020)

green_facades->temperature.source: Street-canyon CFD with facade greening: mean −0.1 K, max −0.3 K, < 0.05 K mid-canyon (engrXiv preprint 2599, https://engrxiv.org/preprint/view/2599); São Paulo ENVI-met: difference at 15 cm from the wall, insignificant from 60 cm (Pós FAUUSP, https://journals.usp.br/posfau/article/view/195441); Cui et al. 2022, PET −0.17 to −1.4 °C near greened facades, Hong Kong (https://ira.lib.polyu.edu.hk/handle/10397/99532); Alexandri & Jones 2008, Building and Environment 43(4):480–493 (https://orca.cardiff.ac.uk/id/eprint/29416/)
green_facades->temperature.notes: 2026-10-29 (one green facade): With one facade the maximum is −0.15 °C (was −0.3 °C for two). Per-building slope unchanged. 2026-10-29 (facade cooling sourced): Slope −2 → −0.15 °C per building: both facades give −0.3 °C. The old −4 °C maximum had no source. Evidence: in a street canyon, greened facades lower air temperature by about 0.1 K on average and 0.3 K at most, under 0.05 K in the middle of the street; field studies find 0.6–1.0 °C only within about a metre of the wall, and a simulation finds no clear difference from 60 cm. The large values in Alexandri & Jones 2008 (up to 8–13 °C) come from a 2D model with green walls and green roofs on whole canyons, mostly in hot climates, which does not fit two buildings at a Berlin junction. About 30–50 % of all facades would be needed for about 1 °C. The stronger effect is local felt comfort next to the wall (PET −0.17 to −1.4 °C, Cui et al. 2022, mainly from greening low on the facade); it is not junction-wide air temperature. Old note: NORMALIZED: max_available_units=2 | max_node_impact=−4°C | slope = max_node_impact / max_available_units = −4 / 2 = −2.000. To change the spawn ceiling (e.g. add a third building), update max_available_units and recalculate slope accordingly. Rationale: 2 buildings with full green facade coverage. Each facade provides insulation + evaporative cooling, −2°C per building.

parking_availability->car_attractivity_g.source: Litman, Transportation Elasticities (VTPI; parking elasticity of car trips −0.1 to −0.3, via FHWA https://ops.fhwa.dot.gov/publications/fhwahop23023/ch2.htm); KonSULT, Univ. of Leeds (halving parking spaces → −30 % car use, model of five English cities, https://its.leeds.ac.uk/projects/konsult/private/level2/instruments/instrument039/l2_039c.htm); kerb share of parking: Hermannstraße count, Berlin (10,480 of about 15,000 spaces, https://api.openstreetmap.org/user/Supaplex030/diary/393423); checks: Amsterdam parking price rise → −2–3 % city traffic (Tinbergen Institute, https://tinbergen.nl/publication/167515/citywide-parking-policy-and-traffic-evidence-from-amsterdam); McCahill et al. 2016 (parking supply causes city-wide driving, https://ssti.us/publications/effects-of-parking-provision-on-automobile-use-in-cities-inferring-causality-mccahill-garrick-atkinson-palombo-and-polinski-2015/).
parking_availability->car_attractivity_g.notes: City scale (2026-10-28). The intersection stands for the whole city, so a driver who loses a space cannot park one street over. Chain: extension on 1/8 = −12 % kerb spaces × 0.7 kerb share of all parking = −8.5 % parking × elasticity 0.3 = −2.5 % car trips. Slope 48 gives −2.51 % in the solver (old slope 18 gave −0.94 %). Today still +6. [FLAG] derived: 0.3 is the middle of 0.1 (Litman; a price elasticity used as a stand-in for scarcity) and 0.6 (KonSULT; a model, not a measurement). [FLAG] estimate: the 0.7 kerb share comes from one Berlin corridor.

cars_replaced_share->car_attractivity_ge.source: Martin & Shaheen 2011 (carsharing member households drive 27–43 % less, https://ops.fhwa.dot.gov/publications/fhwahop16022/ch3.htm); MDPI 2021 Berlin replacement rate (9 cars per shared car); bcs 2023.
cars_replaced_share->car_attractivity_ge.notes: City scale (2026-10-28, replaces the Tier 1 value −3). At city scale the network replaces 54 of 171 parked cars = 32 % of all cars, not a local 1.5 % of traffic. Chain: 32 % of cars × 27 % less driving = −8.6 % car trips. −60 gives −8.7 % in the solver (carsharing alone, against the same run with this term at 0). [FLAG] derived: assumes the replaced cars were driven like average cars; Martin & Shaheen measure whole member households. 27 % is the low end of their range (43 % would give −13.8 %). [FLAG] game scale: at city scale this is a very large programme (a third of all cars replaced, one shared car per 9).

sidewalk_extension_area->pedestrians_sta.source: Fruin 1971 (about 5.5 m² per person, comfortable lingering); this node's 40 % idle-eligible share.
sidewalk_extension_area->pedestrians_sta.notes: 2026-10-29 (greenery on the 11,500 m² map): With 2,700 m² the lingering ceiling rises from about 808 to 966 people. The lingering ceiling grows with new sidewalk area. The existing 4,235 m² is the plaza, so the extension adds on top.

sidewalk_extension_spawn_2->space_activi.source: SF Great Streets Parklet Impact Study (parklets with seating: people stopping and sitting +30 %, https://sf.streetsblog.org/2012/01/05/great-streets-project-quantifies-the-impacts-of-parklets); Whyte 1980 (people sit where there are places to sit); Gehl 2011; Mehta 2007 and 2013 (seating is the strongest street-front driver of lingering).
sidewalk_extension_spawn_2->space_activi.notes: 2026-10-28 (Tier 3 backing): The extension adds activity only together with seating: 0.05 × extension × urban_furniture_share. An empty extension adds 0 (was +11.3); 1 café + half the furniture +1.9 (was +3.7); full furniture +1.0 (unchanged). The studies measured extensions that came with seating. [FLAG] the size 0.05 is still a judgment; the direction and the seating gate are backed. [FLAG] weight 0.05: an extension alone adds about 11 activity points (a third of a café); next to full cafés and furniture about 1 point, so no double counting.

ns_outer_parking_spawn_4->mob_attract_bi.source: Teschke et al. 2012, AJPH 102:2336 (690 injured cyclists, Toronto and Vancouver; major streets without parked cars OR 0.63, with a bike lane OR 0.54), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3519333; dooring share of bike crashes about 15–20 % (Vancouver, Cambridge MA, Chicago), https://dutchreach.org/dooring-problem-prevalence; open door about 1.2 m into the lane.
ns_outer_parking_spawn_4->mob_attract_bi.notes: Dooring: −5.5 while a north-south bike lane runs next to parking on a/f, less with protection, 0 at full protection or with greenery on a/f. Size: ln(0.63) / ln(0.54) = 0.75, so taking parked cars away is worth about three quarters of a bike lane's safety effect; 0.75 × 7.5 points per protection step ≈ 5.5. The east-west street has no term: there a bike lane never runs next to parking. [FLAG] derived: the 7.5 points per step is the model's own scale.

new_bus_stop->mob_attract_bus.source: Walk to transit: median about 290 m, most riders within 400-500 m, demand falls off exponentially with distance (review: https://escholarship.mcgill.ca/downloads/kw52jd240 ; Kimpel et al.: https://escholarship.mcgill.ca/downloads/pr76f844q ; Daniels & Mulley 2013: https://ideas.repec.org/a/kap/transp/v41y2014i1p193-210.html ; Bree, Fuller & Diab 2020: https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/transa/v141y2020icp430-442.html). Walking to the stop is valued about twice a seated minute on the bus (TOI, bus users in five Norwegian cities: https://www.toi.no/publications/bus-passengers-valuation-of-service-improvements-experiences-from-moss-grenland-kristiansand-tromso-and-alesund-article17702-29.html). Scale check: a full stop package (shelter, seats, timetable, real-time info) is worth about 2-4.3 IVT minutes, a shelter alone about 9 % of the fare (Douglas, ATRF 2018: https://australasiantransportresearchforum.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/ATRF2018_paper_84Rev.pdf ; Douglas, NZAE 2017: https://www.nzae.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Douglas-PTQualityRatingSP_NZEA2017_3.pdf); stop upgrades raised boardings about 4 % net (Salt Lake City, https://nitc.trec.pdx.edu/node/5537).
new_bus_stop->mob_attract_bus.notes: +20 while the east-west bus lane is there. See the note on new_bus_stop.

lane_slots.label: East-west street (SP 2 + SP 3), per direction, mirrored
lane_slots.notes: Each lever value is a number of lanes per direction. A layout is buildable when every lane can be given its own slot that fits it. The sidewalk extension fits only on 1/8; parking and sport terrain fill a slot but have no effect in the sim, so they are not listed. A bike lane goes on 1/8, or on 2/7 when 1/8 holds the extension. yields: choosing the extension is never blocked; if the bike lane cannot move to 2/7, the extension replaces it. requires: slot 4/5 can be used only while carsharing >= 1 (a carsharing station at SP 4); until then it stays parking. Game decision (2026-10-28, design team): the extension keeps priority over the bike lane even where a car lane could give way instead. Kept on purpose.

lane_slots.label: North-south street (SP 4), per direction, mirrored
lane_slots.notes: Each lever value is a number of lanes per direction. A layout is buildable when every lane can be given its own slot that fits it. filled: every slot always holds a lane, so car + bike + bus = 2; fill_with: a slot that a bike or bus lane gives up goes back to a car lane, and a bike or bus lane takes its slot from a car lane. The outer lane a/f (parking or greenery with pockets) is not a slot: it sets ns_outer_parking_spawn_4, which drives dooring for a bike lane on b/e.
